sections.title: BCL11B defines a basal-like tumor subpopulation with a preexisting drug resistance ability
sections.text: BCL11B defines a basal-like tumor subpopulation with a preexisting drug resistance abilityHER2 has been identified as an important biomarker and treatment target for a subset of aggressive breast cancers, resulting in the development of highly successful targeted therapy (35). This prompted us to investigate the therapeutic significance of targeting BCL11B in addressing chemoresistance. We first experimentally examined whether the BCL11B-expressing cancer cells have the ability to resist chemotherapeutic drugs. To this end, we used the widely used MMTV-PyMT (PyMT) transgenic mouse model, which has been shown to recapitulate many aspects of human breast cancer (36). Despite being regarded as a luminal type of breast cancer, the primary PyMT tumor harbored a specific subset of KRT14+ basal-like cells, predominantly located at the tumor-stromal border and surrounding KRT8+ luminal tumor cells (Fig. 2A). This finding aligns with observations reported in recent studies (37, 38). Notably, BCL11B+ cells were found to be a notable subset of the KRT14+ population in the tumor (Fig. 2, B and C). These results showed that BCL11B marks a distinctive tumor subpopulation in the PyMT tumor model, exhibiting basal-like features and resembling human BCL11B+ cancer cells.Fig. 2.BCL11B+ cells represent a preexisting drug-resistant cell population.(A) Immunofluorescence costaining of KRT14/KRT8 in primary PyMT tumors. Scale bar, 50 μm. (B) Representative immunostaining images showing KRT14/BCL11B colocalization in PyMT tumors. Scale bar, 50 μm. (C) Mean fraction of KRT14+/− cells within the BCL11B+ population and the mean fraction of BCL11B+/− cells within the KRT14+ population. P < 0.001, one-sample Student’s t test versus 50% (n = 3 tumors). (D) Strategy of the ex vivo drug treatment assay (upper) and representative day 10 tdTomato images of organoids (lower). Scale bars, 200 μm (left) and 100 μm (right). h, hours; d, days. (E) Quantification of the percentage of tdTomato+ cells in tumor organoids; n = 18 organoids from three experiments. (F) WT or Bcl11b KO tumor cells were treated with or without Doxo for 24 hours followed by drug washout. Representative day 11 (D11) images are shown. Scale bar, 300 μm. (G) Quantification of persister organoid frequency (% of control); n = 6 wells from three experiments. (H) KRT14/BCL11B immunostaining in control and drug-resistant WT organoids from (F). Scale bar, 50 μm. (I) Percentage of BCL11B+ cells in tumor organoids under indicated conditions; n = 10 organoids from three experiments. (J) Organoids pregrown for 3 days were treated with Doxo (100 nM) for 7 days followed by drug washout. Representative images are shown. Scale bar, 200 μm. (K) Percentage of actively growing organoids on day 17 in the indicated conditions; n = 6 wells from three experiments. (L) KRT14/BCL11B immunostaining in regrown organoids derived from single-cell dissociation of drug-resistant organoids. Scale bar, 50 μm. (M) Tumor growth curves of WT and Bcl11b KO tumors upon saline or combination treatment [Doxo + cyclophosphamide (AC)]. n = 6 mice per group, two-way ANOVA. Nuclei were counterstained with DAPI (blue). Data are presented as the means ± SEM. ***P < 0.001.To directly test whether the BCL11B+ cancer cell subpopulation has a preexisting capability to resist treatment, we generated the Bcl11b reporter model by crossing the Bcl11btdTomato knockin mice (with an IRES-tdTomato cassette inserted at the 3′ untranslated region of the Bcl11b locus) (39) to MMTV-PyMT mice. Bcl11btdTomato-positive cells represented a small subpopulation of tumor cells in the primary tumor, as revealed by flow cytometric analysis (fig. S3A). We next established an ex vivo drug treatment assay using single-cell suspensions derived from the primary tumors. This assay was designed to test whether a preexisting cell population exists that can resist treatment. Briefly, single epithelial cell adhesion molecule–positive (EpCAM+) tumor cells were sorted from PyMT-Bcl11btdTomato reporter tumors (containing a mixture of tdTomato+ cells and tdTomato− cells) and cultured in Matrigel for 24 hours in the absence or presence of doxorubicin (Doxo), one of the most widely used chemotherapy agents for treating breast cancer (40). The drug was then washed out, and the cells were assayed for their capacity to form tumor organoids, a model system that has been shown to retain key properties of primary tumors (Fig. 2D) (41). In the vehicle-treated control group, PyMT tumor cells robustly grew into organoids within a short period of time (3 to 4 days) (Fig. 2D). However, following Doxo treatment, only a small fraction of cells survived and gradually developed into organoids, which became evident after 7 days (Fig. 2D). Notably, when we analyzed the tdTomato fluorescence, we observed that the drug-resistant persister organoids were almost exclusively composed of Bcl11btdTomato-positive cells, whereas only a minor subset of cells expressed tdTomato in the control organoids (Fig. 2, D and E). To further confirm the tdTomato+ persister organoids derived from preexisting Bcl11b-positive cells, we used fluorescence-activated cell sorting (FACS) to purify single tdTomato+ and tdTomato− cells from untreated reporter organoids and performed the same drug treatment assay. The results suggest that preexisting resistance is the primary driver of survival, as sorted tdTomato+ cells yielded a significantly higher number of persister organoids compared to their tdTomato− counterparts (P < 0.001) (fig. S3B). tdTomato− cells also generated a small number of persister organoids. Notably, these rare surviving organoids consistently regained Bcl11btdTomato expression (fig. S3C), potentially reflecting plastic state switching from a BCL11B− to BCL11B⁺ state, as also occurs during normal cell passaging. Nevertheless, achieving the BCL11B+ state appears to confer chemotherapy persistence.To explore whether Bcl11b is functionally required for the drug-resistant ability of this tumor population, we generated Bcl11b knockout (KO) tumor organoids by CRISPR-Cas9 (fig. S3D). Bcl11b deficiency did not cause an obvious change in the survival of the tumor organoids under normal conditions but led to a near-complete elimination of persister organoids following treatment (P < 0.001) (Fig. 2, F and G, and fig. S3E). Note that under control conditions, Bcl11b KO organoids tended to cluster toward the center of the Matrigel bedding, which limited the volumetric expansion of individual KO organoids at later stages, although the total number of growing organoids remained comparable to wild type (WT) (Fig. 2F). Immunostaining analysis of the persister cells derived from WT tumor cells after treatment revealed that KRT14 and BCL11B double-positive cells were highly enriched in these organoids (Fig. 2, H and I). By contrast, the BCL11B+/KRT14+ tumor cells only constituted a subset of WT control organoids (Fig. 2, H and I). Together, these results reveal that BCL11B+ tumor cells constitute a preexisting drug-tolerant population that can selectively persist during chemotherapy treatment.To study the effects of prolonged treatment, we further administered Doxo to pregrown WT or Bcl11b-deficient tumor organoids for 7 days (Fig. 2J). Most of tumor organoids in both groups demonstrated a decrease in size following the treatment, although a small number of slow-growing organoids were observed in the WT group (Fig. 2J). Notably, upon termination of the treatment, a significant portion of the organoids in the WT group resumed growth, whereas the Bcl11b-deficient organoids were lost over time (Fig. 2, J and K). We also found that the absence of Bcl11b rendered tumor cells much more sensitive to paclitaxel (taxane), another drug commonly used to treat breast cancer (40), highlighting the multiple-drug resistance capacity of the BCL11B-expressing cells (fig. S3, F and G). We then asked whether the persister cells maintain a stable phenotype upon the discontinuation of drug treatment. To eliminate any potential negative impacts of residual drugs and to ensure that any organoids were clonally derived from BCL11B+ cells, we dissociated the persister organoids into single cells and re-embedded them in fresh Matrigel. In the regrown organoids, the percentage of KRT14+/BCL11B+ cells dropped to a level similar to that of the pretreatment organoids (Fig. 2L and fig. S3H), implying the differentiation of BCL11B+ cells. Moreover, the regrown organoids remained responsive to Doxo treatment because of the presence of drug-sensitive BCL11B− cells (fig. S3, I and J). This indicates that BCL11B+ cells drive a reversible cancer persistence under drug treatment.To test whether BCL11B expression enables tumor cells to establish a drug-resistant ability, we reintroduced BCL11B expression in the Bcl11b KO organoid cells (fig. S3K). We found that the restoration of BCL11B expression induced a de novo drug resistance phenotype in these cells (fig. S3, K to M). To further confirm the role of BCL11B in vivo, we grew tumors from WT and Bcl11b KO PyMT cells in mice and performed a drug treatment study. Consistent with our in vitro findings, KO of Bcl11b significantly increased the antitumor efficacy of either Doxo alone or the commonly used combination chemotherapy [adriamycin (Doxo) combined with cyclophosphamide (AC)] (P < 0.001) (Fig. 2M and fig. S4A). At the histological level, Bcl11b KO tumors exhibited a marked reduction in overall viability and a significant loss of Ki67+ proliferating cells 6 days after the final chemotherapy treatment. In contrast, proliferating cells remained readily detectable throughout chemotherapy-treated WT tumors, including residual regions with high Ki67 positivity (fig. S4, B and C). Furthermore, while TUNEL (terminal deoxynucleotidyl transferase–mediated deoxyuridine triphosphate nick end labeling) assays revealed distinct areas of apoptosis in WT tumors after treatment, the drug-treated KO tumors were predominantly composed of completely necrotic tissue lacking intact nuclei [4′,6-diamidino-2-phenylindole (DAPI)–negative] (fig. S4B). Drug treatment also induced an obvious enrichment of BCL11B+ cells and KRT14+ cells in the WT residual tumor (fig. S4, D and E), consistent with the role of BCL11B in mediating treatment resistance. Last, to determine whether WT persister cells remaining after treatment have tumor-regenerating potential in vivo and whether Bcl11b deletion abolishes this ability, we treated WT or Bcl11b KO organoids ex vivo with Doxo for 7 days, as shown in Fig. 2J, and transplanted equal numbers of residual tumor cells into recipient mice. Consistent with our in vitro findings, chemotherapy-treated WT cells readily reestablished tumors upon transplantation. In contrast, drug-treated Bcl11b KO cells completely failed to initiate any detectable tumor growth throughout the entire 10-week observation period (P < 0.001) (fig. S4F). Together, these in vitro and in vivo observations suggest that BCL11B shapes a preexisting tumor population that is tolerant to multiple chemotherapeutic drugs and drives cancer persistence upon treatment.

sections.title: The Bcl11b+ cell state is intrinsically associated with drug-resistant properties
sections.text: The Bcl11b+ cell state is intrinsically associated with drug-resistant propertiesTo investigate how Bcl11b+ cells are primed to adopt a drug-resistant state, we first performed bulk RNA sequencing (RNA-seq) analysis on Bcl11b+ and Bcl11b− cells in treatment-naïve tumors. As expected, basal genes such as Col17a1, Krt14, and Krt5 were highly expressed by Bcl11b+ cells, while luminal markers were predominantly observed in Bcl11b− cells (Fig. 3A and table S2). However, many of the top enriched genes in Bcl11b+ cells, such as Dsc3, Dsg3, and Tgfbi, have not been previously linked to mammary basal cells. Conversely, markers associated with a more mature myoepithelial phenotype, including Actg2, Myh11, Myl9, and Mylk, were found to be expressed at low levels in Bcl11b+ cells (Fig. 3B), consistent with our observations in human BCL11B+ cells. Kyoto Encyclopedia of Genes and Genomes (KEGG) pathway analysis further uncovered an enrichment of genes involved in xenobiotic metabolism and glutathione (GSH) metabolism in the treatment-naïve Bcl11b+ cells, such as Aldh3a1, Cyp26a1, and Mgst2 (Fig. 3, C and D). Both pathways have been closely associated with detoxifying chemotherapeutic drugs in cancer (42, 43). Notably, one of the representative genes, the aldehyde dehydrogenase enzyme Aldh3a1, has been demonstrated in breast cancer to protect cells against various chemotherapeutic drugs including Doxo, paclitaxel, and cyclophosphamide (44, 45). By interrogating a recent single-cell transcriptome atlas spanning mouse mammary development stages (46), we also unexpectedly identified that Bcl11b and its associated gene program in cancer were specifically enriched in the rudimentary basal-like cells at the early postnatal stage (day 5) (Fig. 3E and fig. S5, A to C). Most of basal-like cells at this early postnatal stage lacked myoepithelial markers (Fig. 3E) and represented a precursor population in an intermediate developmental stage (14, 47). Many of the xenobiotic detoxification genes also showed a specific enrichment in this early basal cell state (Fig. 3E and fig. S5C). Therefore, these results suggest that Bcl11b+ tumor cells mimic a precursor-like developmental state in cancer, which is inherently linked to a xenobiotic inactivation program that may play a physiological role in responding to external stimuli.Fig. 3.BCL11B functionally governs an immature basal-like cell state with inherent drug resistance abilities.(A) Volcano plot showing genes differentially expressed between Bcl11b+ and Bcl11b− PyMT tumor cells. (B) Heatmap visualization of general basal marker genes and myoepithelial-enriched genes in the bulk RNA-seq dataset of Bcl11b+ and Bcl11b− tumor cells. (C) KEGG pathway analysis of the up-regulated genes in Bcl11b+ PyMT tumor cells. (D) Heatmap showing the expression levels of representative drug resistance genes in the bulk RNA-seq data of Bcl11b+ and Bcl11b− cells. (E) UMAP plots displaying the expression patterns of indicated genes in the scRNA-seq dataset of mammary basal and basal-like cells spanning four developmental stages: embryonic, early postnatal, prepuberty, and adult. (F) Representative images of WT and Bcl11b KO tumor organoids. Panels display bright-field imaging (left), KRT14/BCL11B costaining (middle), and KRT8 staining (right). Scale bar, 50 μm. (G) Quantification of the percentage of KRT14+ cells in WT and Bcl11b KO organoids; n = 15 organoids from three experiments. (H) Real-time PCR analysis of indicated genes in WT and Bcl11b KO tumor cells with Actb as an internal control; n = 3 experiments. (I) UMAP representation of 3377 vehicle-treated tumor organoid cells. The cells are colored by clusters. (J) UMAP plots displaying the expression patterns of the indicated genes in the control organoid cells. (K) Box plot showing the CytoTRACE scores of indicated tumor populations (Wilcoxon rank-sum test). Nuclei were counterstained with DAPI (blue). Data are presented as the means ± SEM. **P < 0.01 and ***P < 0.001.Given that the deficiency of Bcl11b compromised the drug resistance ability, we questioned whether Bcl11b is functionally required for maintaining the immature basal-like cell state and its associated drug resistance program. The loss of Bcl11b resulted in a substantial decrease in the number of KRT14+ tumor cells, both in vitro and in vivo, while leaving the KRT8+ luminal cell lineage unaffected (Fig. 3, F and G, and fig. S5, D and E). The mRNA levels of Krt14 and the drug resistance genes, including Aldh3a1, Cyp26a1, and Mgst2, were also significantly down-regulated in tumor organoids after the KO of Bcl11b (Fig. 3H). Transcriptomic analysis of WT and Bcl11b KO tumor organoids further confirmed that both the basal gene program and drug resistance program were impaired upon the deletion of Bcl11b (fig. S5F and table S3). Moreover, we used a recently published BCL11B binding dataset generated in the same PyMT tumor model (48) and identified BCL11B binding at the Krt14 promoter, as well as at the promoter regions of other downstream genes such as Aldh3a1 and Mgst2, suggesting that these genes are direct downstream targets of BCL11B (fig. S5G). To validate these findings, we performed a CUT&RUN (cleavage under targets and release using nuclease) assay in our PyMT tumor organoids and confirmed BCL11B binding at the Aldh3a1 promoter in control organoids, with loss of this binding upon Bcl11b deletion (fig. S5H). We also detected BCL11B binding at the promoter of Snai2 (fig. S5G), a key regulator in the mammary epithelium that controls basal/stem cell maintenance. Snai2 expression was also markedly down-regulated upon Bcl11b deletion (table S3), indicating that BCL11B may also regulate the basal-like cell state indirectly through Snai2. Together, these results suggest that Bcl11b functionally controls an immature basal-like cell state that is inherently linked to a preexisting drug detoxification gene program and exhibits selective advantages upon chemotherapy treatment.

sections.title: Analysis of human breast cancer scRNA-seq datasets
sections.text: Analysis of human breast cancer scRNA-seq datasetsWe obtained scRNA-seq data from two publicly available human breast cancer datasets (26, 92). Metaplastic breast tumors were excluded from the analysis because they exhibit distinct biological, histopathological, and transcriptional characteristics compared with conventional invasive breast cancers. After filtering out low-quality cells on the basis of mitochondrial gene percentage and the number of detected RNA features, malignant cells were used for downstream CytoTRACE analysis. Malignant cell annotations based on InferCNV analysis were obtained either from the original studies or from processed datasets included in a published integrated single-cell atlas of human breast cancer (93). CytoTRACE analysis was performed in R using the publicly available CytoTRACE package (https://cytotrace.stanford.edu).

sections.title: Organoid culture
sections.text: Organoid cultureTwenty microliters of growth factor–reduced Matrigel (BD Bioscience) was added to a well of a round-bottom 96-well plate and allowed to solidify at 37°C for 10 min. FACS-sorted tumor cells were then resuspended in 150 μl of organoid culture media [Advanced DMEM/F-12 + 2% FBS + PSA + N2 + B27 + 10 mM Hepes + EGF (10 ng/ml; Invitrogen) + Rspo1 (250 ng/ml; R&D) + ROCK inhibitor Y27632 (10 μM; Sigma-Aldrich) + Noggin (100 ng/ml; R&D)] and overlaid on top of the Matrigel. Organoids were grown in humidified tissue culture incubators at 37°C in 5% CO2 and were supplemented every 2 or 3 days with fresh media. For passaging, organoids were first incubated in a prechilled cell recovery solution (Corning) on ice for 20 min and then dissociated into single cells by trypsin digestion.For lentivirus-mediated gene knockdown, organoid cells were transduced with scrambled virus (Sigma-Aldrich), Aldh3a1, or Abcb1b short hairpin RNA virus that was produced in 293T cells, as described previously (94). Single organoid cells were mixed with a concentrated lentiviral supernatant (to a multiplicity of infection of 20) in organoid culture media with polybrene (4 μg/ml; Sigma-Aldrich) and incubated in a 48-well nonadherent culture plate overnight. The next day, cells were washed and cultured on Matrigel in normal organoid media. Seventy-two hours later, positive cell selection was started by puromycin addition.

sections.title: CRISPR-mediated genome editing in tumor organoids
sections.text: CRISPR-mediated genome editing in tumor organoidsGuide RNA targeting exon 1 of Bcl11b (CCGGGCAATGTCCCGCCGCAAACAGG) was cloned into the Cas9-containing lentiCRISPR v2 vector. Lentivirus production and transfection were performed as described above. After infection, single tumor cells from primary tumors were plated on Matrigel for organoid culture, followed by selection with puromycin. Single organoid clones were then isolated and expanded. Genomic DNA was isolated from the selected clones, and the targeted mutation in the Bcl11b locus was confirmed by Sanger sequencing. Two single organoid clones were verified through immunostaining and subsequently used for the experiments. To ensure genetic stability and minimize potential culture-induced artifacts inherent to primary cells, all downstream experiments were performed using these validated organoid clones within six passages.

sections.title: RNA isolation and real-time PCR
sections.text: RNA isolation and real-time PCRTotal RNA was extracted with the RNeasy Plus Micro Kit (Qiagen) and reverse transcribed to cDNA using the SuperScript III First Strand Synthesis kit (Life Technologies) according to the manufacturer’s instructions. Real-time polymerase chain reaction (PCR) was performed on the 7900HT Fast Real-Time PCR System (Applied Biosystems) or QuantStudio 7 PRO Real-Time PCR System (Thermo Fisher Scientific) using Power SYBR Green PCR Master Mix (Life Technologies). Gapdh or Actb was used to normalize the expression values. PCR primers are listed in table S7.

sections.title: RNA-seq and data processing
sections.text: RNA-seq and data processingTwenty to 100 ng of total RNA was used to generate barcoded RNA-seq libraries using the NEBNext Single Cell/Low Input RNA Library Prep Kit for Illumina (New England Biolabs) following the manufacturer’s instructions. Libraries were sequenced on a NextSeq 550 (Illumina) or HiSeq 2500 (Illumina) to generate 75–base pair (bp) SE reads or 76-bp PE reads. The quality of trimmed Fastq reads was assessed using FastQC. HISAT2 was then used to align the RNA-seq reads to the mouse reference genome (mm10), followed by gene count quantification using htseq-count (95, 96). Alternatively, RNA-seq results were aligned to the mouse reference genome (mm10) and quantified using Salmon (97). Count matrices were analyzed with DESeq2 (98) or Degust (http://degust.erc.monash.edu). Heatmaps were generated using Morpheus software (Broad Institute). KEGG pathway analysis was performed using EnrichR (http://amp.pharm.mssm.edu/Enrichr/).

sections.title: Single-cell RNA sequencing
sections.text: Single-cell RNA sequencingPregrown tumor organoids were treated with or without Doxo (100 nM) for 24 hours. After the treatment, tumor organoids were recovered from Matrigel and digested into single cells using 0.25% trypsin-EDTA (Gibco) supplemented with deoxyribonuclease I for 15 min at 37°C. Freshly sorted live single cells were counted and loaded onto the Chromium Controller (10x Genomics). Each sample was loaded into a separate channel on the Single Cell 3′ Chip targeting 3000 cells. Libraries were prepared using the Chromium Single Cell 3′ Reagent kits v3 (10x Genomics) following the manufacturer’s recommendations. The multiplexed libraries were loaded on a NovaSeq 6000 (Illumina), and paired-end reads were produced using a 200-cycle kit. Each sample was sequenced to an average depth of ∼40,000 read pairs per cell.

sections.title: scRNA-seq data bioinformatic analysis
sections.text: scRNA-seq data bioinformatic analysisThe Cell Ranger pipeline was used to process the raw sequencing data, producing count matrices initially containing 3509 cells in the control group and 3576 cells in the Doxo group. Package Seurat version 4 was used in R to perform downstream analyses (99). Gene signature scores for the “Basal signature,” “Luminal signature,” “Myoepithelial signature,” and “TNF signaling activity” were calculated using the AddModuleScore function in Seurat. The “TNF signaling activity” is composed of the TNF signaling genes in the HALLMARK_TNFA_SIGNALING_VIA_NFKB gene set. Single-cell level prediction of differentiation states in tumor organoid cells was performed in R using the CytoTRACE package publicly available at https://cytotrace.stanford.edu. Single-sample enrichment of the “Normal Basal Signature,” “Normal Luminal Signature,” and dbEMT (100) gene sets was analyzed using ssGSEA, as implemented in the escape package (101). Signature genes (top 200 differentially expressed genes for each lineage) for basal and luminal cells from normal mammary glands were obtained from publicly available RNA-seq data (102), as described in the previous study (103).

sections.title: Data, code, and materials availability:
sections.text: Data, code, and materials availability:All data and code needed to evaluate and reproduce the results in the paper are present in the paper and/or the Supplementary Materials. The scRNA-seq and bulk RNA-seq data generated in this study have been deposited in the Gene Expression Omnibus (GEO) with the primary accession code GSE228442 (www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/geo/query/acc.cgi?acc=GSE228442). Previously published scRNA-seq data that were reanalyzed here are available at GEO under accession codes GSE109774 (www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/geo/query/acc.cgi?acc=GSE109774), GSE176078 (www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/geo/query/acc.cgi?acc=GSE176078), GSE161529 (www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/geo/query/acc.cgi?acc=GSE161529), and GSE164017 (www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/geo/query/acc.cgi?acc=GSE164017). Previous microarray expression data reanalyzed here are available at GEO under accession code GSE6883 (www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/geo/query/acc.cgi?acc=GSE6883). All bioinformatics analyses were performed using publicly available tools. This paper does not report original code. Plasmids generated in this study are available from the corresponding author M.F.C. (mfclarke@stanford.edu) upon reasonable request.
